parakeet: We've all heard it. Christianity is about loving everyone. It's the bumper sticker slogan, the sermon soundbite, the PR line that makes the faith sound universal and humanitarian. But what happens when we actually read the text and trace the tradition? We discover that love thy neighbor never meant what we think it means. In Leviticus, neighbor meant fellow Israelites, your kin, not humanity at large. Jesus redefined family, but only for those who do the will of the Father, making love conditional on obedience. And John went further still, commanding believers not to love the world at all, dividing humanity into children of God and children of the devil. The through line is clear. From Moses to Jesus to John, the ethic of love is never universal. It is always bounded. It's not love without limits, but love within walls. Let's start with the source that Jesus is citing. The text itself is Leviticus chapter 19, verse 18. You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the Lord. Note how the verse ties neighbor directly to the sons of your own people. The command is explicitly framed in reference to fellow Israelites. The key Hebrew word here is rea, which means neighbor, companion, or associate. In the Torah, this term almost always denotes someone in your community or covenant group, not a random outsider.
